From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter
Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of
Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and
look forward to your mark-up.
SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)
Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims
is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.
Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and
only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the
basket is recoverable.
Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after
Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims
unless expressly stated otherwise.
Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same
caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.
Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and
non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.
Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public
registers (see Disclosure Letter).
Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the
Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or
public records.
Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller
will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the
counterparty's written consent.
Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding)
will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.
Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing
bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds
flow.)
Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio
matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.
Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter
and is not expected to be material.
Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course
operating costs.
Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime
above.
Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.
Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and
records are fictional.
1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the
indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including
DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly
searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific
disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent,
payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.
2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause
11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final
written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.
3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2.
As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security
is included.
4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of
every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of
non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.
5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject
to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft
Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or
on-costs apply.
6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external
email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity
timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised
person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation
remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no
loss amount.
7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as
a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.
8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each
(AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether
each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.
9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale
consent is required merely because shares are sold.
10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of
the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the
Buyer has completed its own verification.
11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer
must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

# Project Kestrel — Buyer-Side Review of Seller Update and Disclosure Letter (SPA-003)

**Prepared for:** Wattlebridge Holdings deal team
**Basis:** 100% of Paperbark Analytics; AUD 24,000,000; debt-free/cash-free; NSW law
**Status of material reviewed:** Seller's draft positions — treated as adversarial, not accepted

---

## Executive view

The Seller's package is not "fair and balanced". It combines (a) a liability regime that would make most realistic claims unrecoverable, (b) a disclosure mechanism that shifts almost all known risk to us without giving us a price or indemnity adjustment, and (c) a set of known, quantifiable exposures — Riverlark debt, closing bonuses, Ironquay IP, the DD-006 incident, Bluefen consent — that the Seller is attempting to park either outside the funds flow or outside any meaningful remedy.

The disclosure letter itself is unusually candid about *what is missing* (no Bluefen consent, no Riverlark discharge, no Ironquay receipt, bonuses not in funds flow). That candour should be read as the Seller building a knowledge/disclosure defence under clause 8.3 and Schedule 7, not as an offer to solve anything. Our job is to turn each of those admissions into a closing deliverable, a price adjustment, or a specific indemnity.

Roughly AUD 4.1 million of known leakage or exposure (Riverlark ~3.2m, bonuses 0.42m + on-costs, Ironquay 0.18m, Sandbar 0.33m) sits in the Seller's draft without clear allocation to the Seller, against a headline price of 24m. That is before any valuation hit on Bluefen (30% of revenue) or DD-006.

---

## Part A — Liability architecture (clauses 8.3, 9.3, 12, 13, 20.5)

### A1. Fundamental and title warranties subjected to general caps and time limits — **reject outright**

The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties share the 20% cap and 18‑month period "for administrative simplicity". That is not a simplification; it is the single most buyer‑adverse term in the package.

- If title to the shares fails, we have paid AUD 24m for nothing. A recovery ceiling of AUD 4.8m is absurd for that risk.
- Market position (and what any Australian buyer would expect): title, capacity, authority and (usually) tax warranties capped at **100% of the purchase price** and surviving for the longer of the statutory limitation period or 6–7 years (tax: typically until expiry of the relevant assessment periods plus a margin).
- Note the disclosure letter paragraph 10: the Seller says title is "evidenced by the Company share register at DD‑012" and expressly notes that this "does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification." Read with clause 8.3, that is a set‑up: the Seller is laying the ground to argue that any title defect discoverable from the register or ASIC records was within our knowledge and is barred. Title must be an uncapped, un‑excludable warranty *and* backed by completion deliverables (executed transfers, register update, ASIC lodgement, share certificates or cancellation, no‑encumbrance confirmation).

**Ask:** Separate "Fundamental Warranties" (title, capacity, authority, no insolvency, solvency, share capital) — cap 100% of price, survive 7 years, excluded from basket/de minimis, excluded from knowledge qualifier and from disclosure. Tax warranties and tax indemnity — cap 100%, survive 7 years (or 4 years after end of the last relevant amendment period).

### A2. General cap at 20% (AUD 4.8m) — **negotiate up; acceptable only as part of a package**

20% is at the low end of the Australian mid‑market range (typically 20–50% for a company of this size with identified risk concentration). Given that 30% of revenue hinges on a single customer consent and there is an open privacy incident, we should open at 50% and expect to land at 30–35%, with specific indemnities sitting *outside* the cap (see Part B). If the Seller holds at 20%, the trade is W&I insurance with the Seller funding part of the premium, or a retention/escrow.

### A3. De minimis AUD 25,000 and basket AUD 250,000 (excess‑only) — **reduce and convert**

- De minimis of 25k on a 24m deal is roughly 0.1% — high but tolerable. Push to 10–15k and, critically, insist that **related claims aggregate** for de minimis purposes. Otherwise the three Sandbar renewals (3 × 110k) and a series of DD‑006 remediation costs can each be argued separately.
- Basket of 250k (~1.04%) is at the top of market. Push for 0.5–0.75%, and convert from "excess only" (deductible) to **"tipping"/first‑dollar** once exceeded.
- Confirm de minimis and basket **do not apply** to Fundamental, Tax, or specific indemnity claims, nor to the leakage/purchase‑price adjustment mechanics.

### A4. 18‑month claims period — **extend**

18 months is short for a software/analytics business where IP and data issues surface slowly. Ask for 24 months for general warranties (minimum: 18 months plus a window that captures at least one full audit cycle after Completion). Tax and Fundamental as per A1.

### A5. "Any limitation applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise" (cl 12.3/13) and "limitations, exclusive remedy and non‑reliance apply to all Claims of any nature" (cl 9.3/12.8/20.5) — **reject the drafting; carve out**

These are catch‑all provisions designed to sweep indemnities, covenants, leakage claims and even fraud into the capped regime. Required carve‑outs from *all* limitations:

1. Fraud, dishonesty, wilful concealment, wilful breach.
2. Fundamental and Tax Warranties / Tax Indemnity (own regime).
3. Specific indemnities (Part B) — subject only to their own caps, if any.
4. Leakage and purchase‑price adjustment claims (locked box or completion accounts mechanics must sit outside the cap and basket entirely).
5. Seller covenants (restraints, confidentiality, pre‑completion conduct, completion deliverables).
6. Liability that cannot be excluded at law — in particular, **statutory misleading or deceptive conduct claims** (Australian Consumer Law / ASIC Act). A clause purporting to exclude these is of doubtful enforceability but it will be run against us; make the carve‑out explicit.

Non‑reliance (20.5) must be mutual in effect — i.e., it should not operate to deny us reliance on the warranties, disclosure letter, or any management responses given in a formal Q&A process. Those should be expressly listed as reliance material.

Exclusive remedy (12.8) must not exclude injunctive relief, specific performance (critical for the completion deliverables in Part B), or rescission for fraud.

### A6. Buyer knowledge qualifier (cl 8.3) — **reject in the Seller's form**

As drafted, we lose any claim for any matter "discoverable from the data room or public records". That means:

- Every item the Seller has itself flagged in paragraphs 2–10 of the disclosure letter is, on the Seller's drafting, barred — including items the Seller admits are *unresolved* and unquantified (DD‑006, Ironquay, bonus on‑costs).
- "Discoverable" is a constructive‑knowledge standard; "advisers" extends it to things our lawyers *could* have found in ASIC searches. This is not market.
- It is an anti‑sandbagging clause at its most aggressive.

**Position:**

- Preferred: delete 8.3 entirely (pro‑sandbagging silence). Fall‑back: actual knowledge only, of a named deal team (3–4 individuals), of a matter *and* of the fact that it gives rise to a breach, and with no imputation from advisers.
- Whatever the knowledge standard, it must not apply to matters that are the subject of a specific indemnity — we know about those by definition; that is precisely why we are indemnifying them.

### A7. General disclosure of the data room and public registers (Schedule 7 / DL 1.1–1.2) — **reject; require fair disclosure standard**

Wholesale disclosure of an entire data room (DD‑002 to DD‑012) and of "publicly searchable corporate records" is not an acceptable disclosure standard. Require:

- Disclosure only of matters **fairly disclosed with sufficient detail to enable a reasonable buyer to identify the nature and scope of the matter**.
- Public registers: at most, ASIC company search and PPSR search against the Company as at a specified date, and only for the matters actually revealed on the face of those searches.
- Data room disclosed only against the warranties to which the document is relevant, by cross‑reference in the disclosure letter.
- Data room cut‑off at 22 September 2026 is fine, but documents loaded late, or buried in the wrong folder, must be flagged in a supplementary disclosure letter or not count.
- Paragraph 1.4 (no admission of breach, liability, materiality, or that anything is "legally required") is standard but must not be allowed to blunt the specific indemnities. We should respond in the SPA: "The Seller acknowledges that the matters in paragraphs 2–8 of the Disclosure Letter are the subject of the Specific Indemnities and that disclosure does not limit those indemnities."

Also note the Seller's reservation at paragraph 11: "The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement." Taken with 8.3 and 1.1, this is the Seller attempting to transfer the entire burden of diligence conclusions to us while retaining none of the risk. We should put on record (in correspondence, not just the SPA) that we are relying on the Seller's warranties and the specific indemnities, and that disclosure of a problem is not resolution of it.

---

## Part B — Identified exposures and how each should be allocated

### B1. Bluefen (DD‑002; ~AUD 3.6m, ~30% of FY26 revenue) — **make it a genuine condition precedent with teeth**

Seller position: "addressed"; reasonable endeavours; condition "satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent."

Problems:

- The disclosure letter admits no final written consent exists and no evidence that the clause 11.3 conditions have been satisfied. The Seller cannot describe the matter as "addressed".
- "Reasonable endeavours" is the weakest endeavours standard. For the customer that is 30% of revenue, we need "all reasonable endeavours" at minimum and ideally "best endeavours", with specific steps and reporting obligations.
- "Satisfied on delivery of written consent" is too loose: Bluefen could deliver a consent that is conditional, time‑limited, requires renegotiated pricing, or waives change‑control only in part.

**Ask:**

- CP (for the Buyer's sole benefit, waivable only by the Buyer): unconditional written consent from Bluefen under clause 11.2 in a form approved by the Buyer (acting reasonably), confirming the clause 11.3 conditions are satisfied or waived, with no amendment to commercial terms, and not withdrawn as at Completion.
- Buyer right to participate in communications with Bluefen; Seller not to make commitments on the Company's behalf without consent.
- If the consent is not obtained by the long‑stop date: Buyer may terminate, or elect to complete with a **price reduction** or **deferred/contingent consideration** tied to Bluefen revenue retention over 12–24 months (a 30% customer justifies this).
- Specific indemnity for loss if Bluefen terminates or materially reduces volumes within [12] months citing the change of control.
- Warranty: no notice (written or oral) from Bluefen of intention to terminate, reduce, re‑tender or renegotiate.

### B2. Riverlark Bank facility (DD‑003; ~AUD 3.2m) — **must be discharged at or before Completion; it is not a post‑Completion matter**

Seller position: release "to be provided following Completion."

This is inconsistent with the debt‑free/cash‑free basis. If the facility is still outstanding at Completion and the release arrives later, we have, in effect, paid AUD 24m *and* acquired AUD 3.2m of debt — a 13% price increase. Further, DD‑003 contains a change‑of‑control clause (8.1); completing without the bank's consent or repayment may trigger an event of default against the Company we now own.

**Ask:**

- Completion deliverable: executed deed of release and discharge of security from Riverlark, PPSR discharge (or undertaking to discharge within 2 business days with evidence), release of any guarantees given by the Company, and payout letter.
- Funds flow: repayment of the Riverlark payout figure **from the purchase price** at Completion, paid directly to Riverlark by the Buyer on the Seller's behalf. The Seller nets off; the Company closes debt‑free.
- If for any reason the facility is not repaid at Completion, a dollar‑for‑dollar price reduction and a Seller indemnity (uncapped) for all amounts owing, break costs and any default consequences.
- Confirm there are no other financial debts, hire purchase, guarantees or off‑balance‑sheet items under the "debt" definition — warranty plus completion certificate.

### B3. Closing bonuses (DD‑005; AUD 420,000 plus on‑costs) — **Seller cost, in the funds flow, grossed up**

Seller position: "a matter for the Seller and not separately itemised."

The bonuses are payable *by the Company* on Completion and continued employment. If they are not in the funds flow, the Company pays them post‑Completion from cash we have paid for — classic leakage. The disclosure letter openly admits they are not in the funds flow and that payroll tax, superannuation and on‑costs are unstated. Transaction bonuses typically attract superannuation guarantee (if OTE), payroll tax (NSW ~5.45%) and PAYG withholding; the all‑in cost is likely AUD 500–520k, not 420k.

**Ask:**

- Treat all Completion/transaction bonuses, plus employer superannuation, payroll tax and any other on‑costs, as **Transaction Costs / Debt‑like items** deducted from the price, or funded by the Seller into the Company at Completion with a specific line in the funds flow.
- Specific indemnity for any shortfall or any further transaction‑related payments to employees, advisers or management not reflected in the funds flow.
- Because the bonuses are conditioned on continued employment, clarify who bears the cost if the employee resigns before the pay date — it should not become a Buyer cost either way.
- Request the full list of recipients and terms; check for any change‑of‑control acceleration of options/ESOP or notice entitlements elsewhere.

### B4. Ironquay Development Studio (DD‑004 cl 7.3; DD‑010 shows AUD 180,000 open) — **title‑to‑IP issue, not a 180k issue**

Seller position: existing indemnity limited to the SOW3 payment and "considered adequate."

It is not adequate. Clause 7.3 conditions transfer of the SOW3 Project Materials on *cleared payment of every SOW3 fee*. If AUD 180,000 is unpaid, Paperbark does **not own** the SOW3 deliverables — Ironquay does. For an analytics business, that could be core product code. The exposure is not the 180k; it is (a) an IP title gap in the product, (b) Ironquay's leverage to demand more, (c) potential infringement claims for ongoing use, and (d) breach of the IP ownership warranties we would be giving to our own financiers or future buyers.

**Ask:**

- Completion deliverables: evidence of cleared payment of all SOW3 fees (bank confirmation, not just the ledger) **and** a confirmatory deed of assignment from Ironquay of all SOW3 Project Materials, including moral rights consents and source code delivery.
- If not available by Completion: price retention/escrow (say AUD 250–300k) released on delivery of the assignment, plus an uncapped specific indemnity for loss arising from any failure of title to or restriction on use of the SOW3 materials and any claim by Ironquay.
- Expand the indemnity beyond SOW3 — ask for IP‑ownership confirmation across all SOWs with Ironquay and any other contractor.
- IP warranties: Company owns or validly licenses all IP used in the business; all contractor‑developed IP has been assigned in writing; no open‑source copyleft contamination; source code escrow if relevant.

### B5. DD‑006 export / privacy incident — **not "preliminary and immaterial"; treat as live regulatory exposure**

Seller position: "preliminary operational matter… not expected to be material."

Facts the Seller itself discloses: a download link was sent to an unintended external email address; ~1,240 records of personal information (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps); unknown whether accessed; investigation incomplete; notification assessment not done.

Under the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) Notifiable Data Breaches scheme, an entity that suspects an eligible data breach must complete an assessment within 30 days and notify the OAIC and affected individuals if there is likely to be serious harm. The data (business contact details) is lower‑sensitivity, which helps, but the Seller has not done the assessment and the clock is running. The OAIC's enforcement posture and the penalty regime have hardened significantly since the 2022–2024 reforms. There may also be contractual notification obligations to the customer(s) whose users' data is involved — potentially Bluefen or Mossvale — which bears directly on B1.

**Ask:**

- Pre‑Completion covenant: Seller to procure that the Company completes the NDB assessment, documents it, obtains privacy counsel's opinion, and makes any required notifications before Completion; Buyer to receive copies and have approval rights over regulator and customer communications.
- Warranties: no other actual or suspected data breaches; compliance with APPs and contractual data obligations; no regulator correspondence.
- Specific indemnity (outside cap, basket and 8.3 knowledge qualifier) for all loss arising from the DD‑006 incident — regulator action, notification costs, customer claims or terminations, remediation, legal fees — surviving at least 6 years.
- Condition or termination right if the incident escalates to a confirmed breach involving a key customer before Completion.
- Check the Company's cyber insurance: notification given? Claim preserved? Policy survives change of control?

### B6. Sandbar supplier renewals (DD‑008, DD‑011; 3 × AUD 110,000) — **structure smell; investigate before conceding "ordinary course"**

Seller position: ordinary‑course operating costs.

The disclosure letter undercuts the Seller's own position: it says the three renewals must be "read together for timing/scope" and expressly declines to say whether they are "unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course." Three identical AUD 110k commitments, split across two data‑room documents, each just over 4× the de minimis — this looks like a single AUD 330k commitment fragmented, either to stay beneath approval thresholds or to defeat the de minimis if claimed individually.

**Ask:**

- Full copies of all three renewals, signing dates, approval records, and board/management authority. Were they entered after the locked‑box date or during the exclusivity period? If so, they are potentially leakage or breach of pre‑Completion conduct covenants.
- Confirm whether the services are needed; whether they are terminable; whether the counterparties are related to the Seller or management (related‑party warranty).
- If not demonstrably ordinary course and necessary, treat as leakage / price reduction, or require the Seller to procure termination without cost.
- Ensure de minimis aggregation language (A3) captures related claims.

### B7. Office lease (DD‑007) and Mossvale (DD‑009) — **lower priority but close out**

- Lease: a notification obligation on change of control is usually straightforward, but a missed notification can be a default. Make it a pre‑Completion covenant with evidence of delivery as a Completion deliverable; warranty of no landlord default or dispute.
- Mossvale: the Seller is correct that a restriction on *assignment* is not usually triggered by a share sale. But check for any "change of control" definition elsewhere in the contract, any key‑person or ownership representations, and any most‑favoured‑customer or exclusivity terms. Confirm Mossvale's revenue contribution; if it is a top‑5 customer, add it to the Bluefen‑style no‑notice warranty.

### B8. Tax and IP "settled under the general regime" — **not accepted**

The Seller's one‑liner is a placeholder for "no tax indemnity, no separate IP regime." For a software company with contractor‑developed IP (Ironquay) and a debt facility, we need:

- Full tax indemnity (pre‑Completion tax, uncapped or 100% of price, 7‑year survival), including GST, payroll tax (relevant to B3), R&D tax incentive clawback risk, and Division 7A/related‑party items.
- Tax warranties outside the general cap and knowledge qualifier.
- IP as above (B4): ownership, assignment chain, no infringement, open‑source compliance, data rights in the analytics datasets.

### B9. Title (DD‑012) — see A1. Add: ASIC and PPSR searches as at Completion; Seller to deliver signed transfers, register updates, resignation/appointments, and a solvency/no‑encumbrance warranty. The disclaimer that we have not verified title is the Seller's problem to cure with warranties, not ours to absorb.

---

## Part C — Structural protections to put on the table

Given the number of unresolved items the Seller has itself identified, we should not rely on warranty claims alone:

1. **Retention / escrow**: 10–15% of price (AUD 2.4–3.6m) held for 18–24 months to secure warranty and indemnity claims. Alternatively, W&I insurance with Seller‑funded premium (noting known issues — Bluefen, DD‑006, Ironquay — will be excluded from cover, which is exactly why they need standalone indemnities and escrow).
2. **Price mechanics**: if locked box, lock the box date, define leakage to include the bonuses, Sandbar renewals (if post‑date) and any Riverlark non‑repayment; if completion accounts, ensure debt definition captures Riverlark, accrued bonuses and on‑costs. Debt‑free/cash‑free must be given mechanical effect, not just recited.
3. **Specific indemnities register** — outside cap, basket, time limits and knowledge qualifier:
   - Riverlark non‑discharge / default
   - Transaction bonuses and on‑costs
   - Ironquay IP title and claims
   - DD‑006 incident
   - Bluefen change‑of‑control loss (or contingent consideration)
   - Pre‑Completion tax
4. **Completion deliverables checklist** — Bluefen consent, Riverlark release/PPSR discharge, Ironquay payment evidence + assignment, lease notification, DD‑006 assessment report, share transfer documents.
5. **Long‑stop date and termination rights** for failure of CPs, MAC (including loss or notice from Bluefen, or regulatory action on DD‑006).
6. **Information covenant** between signing and Completion: weekly updates on Bluefen, Riverlark, DD‑006; no new supplier commitments over AUD 25k without consent.

---

## Summary of recommendations

| # | Issue | Seller position | Our position | Priority |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Fundamental/title warranties | Same cap & period as general | 100% of price; 7 years; outside basket, disclosure and knowledge qualifier | Critical |
| 2 | Buyer knowledge (8.3) | Constructive knowledge incl. advisers, data room, public records | Delete; fallback actual knowledge of named individuals, not applicable to indemnified matters | Critical |
| 3 | Riverlark AUD 3.2m | Release after Completion | Repaid from price at Completion; release & PPSR discharge as deliverables; uncapped indemnity | Critical |
| 4 | Bluefen consent (30% revenue) | "Addressed"; reasonable endeavours | Buyer‑only CP, unconditional consent in approved form; all reasonable/best endeavours; price adjustment or deferred consideration if not obtained; indemnity | Critical |
| 5 | Limitations apply to all Claims | Catch‑all | Carve out fraud, Fundamental, Tax, specific indemnities, leakage, covenants, non‑excludable statutory claims; equitable remedies preserved | Critical |
| 6 | Closing bonuses AUD 420k | Not in funds flow | Seller cost incl. super/payroll tax; in funds flow as price deduction; indemnity | High |
| 7 | Ironquay IP | SOW3 payment indemnity "adequate" | Payment evidence + confirmatory assignment as deliverables; escrow; uncapped IP title indemnity; broader IP warranties | High |
| 8 | DD‑006 incident | Preliminary, immaterial | Pre‑Completion NDB assessment and notifications; specific indemnity outside cap/knowledge; MAC trigger | High |
| 9 | General disclosure | Whole data room + public registers | Fair‑disclosure standard; specific cross‑referenced disclosure; limited searches only | High |
| 10 | General cap 20% | AUD 4.8m | Open 50%, land 30–35%; or W&I + escrow | High |
| 11 | De minimis/basket | 25k / 250k deductible | 10–15k with aggregation / 0.5–0.75% tipping | Medium |
| 12 | Claims period | 18 months | 24 months general; 7 years Fundamental & Tax | Medium |
| 13 | Sandbar renewals | Ordinary course | Full diligence; leakage/price reduction unless demonstrably necessary and pre‑existing | Medium |
| 14 | Tax/IP regimes | "Settled" under general regime | Standalone tax indemnity and tax/IP warranties outside general cap | Medium |
| 15 | Lease / Mossvale | Notification only / no consent | Covenants and deliverables; confirm no CoC triggers | Low |
| 16 | Escrow/security | None offered | 10–15% retention 18–24 months or W&I with Seller‑funded premium | High |

**Recommended next steps:** (1) Issue a mark‑up that re‑cuts the liability regime per Part A before engaging on individual items — the Seller's package only works for them if 8.3 and the "all Claims" sweep survive. (2) Send a focused information request: Bluefen correspondence, Riverlark payout letter, Ironquay payment evidence, bonus schedule with on‑costs, DD‑006 investigation file and insurer notification, the three Sandbar agreements with signing dates. (3) Have the valuation team model a Bluefen‑loss scenario and a Riverlark‑not‑repaid scenario so we go into the call with the price impact in hand. (4) Put on record, in correspondence, that we are relying on the warranties and specific indemnities notwithstanding the Seller's reservation at paragraph 11.

I'm happy to turn any of the above into SPA drafting or a rider to the disclosure letter response.

# Project Kestrel — Buyer-Side Review of Seller Update and Disclosure Letter (SPA-003)

**Prepared for:** Wattlebridge Holdings deal team
**Basis:** 100% of Paperbark Analytics; AUD 24,000,000; debt-free/cash-free; NSW law
**Status of material reviewed:** Seller's draft positions — treated as adversarial, not accepted

---

## Executive view

The Seller's package is not "fair and balanced". It combines (a) a liability regime that would make most realistic claims unrecoverable, (b) a disclosure mechanism that shifts almost all known risk to us without giving us a price or indemnity adjustment, and (c) a set of known, quantifiable exposures — Riverlark debt, closing bonuses, Ironquay IP, the DD-006 incident, Bluefen consent — that the Seller is attempting to park either outside the funds flow or outside any meaningful remedy.

The disclosure letter itself is unusually candid about *what is missing* (no Bluefen consent, no Riverlark discharge, no Ironquay receipt, bonuses not in funds flow). That candour should be read as the Seller building a knowledge/disclosure defence under clause 8.3 and Schedule 7, not as an offer to solve anything. Our job is to turn each of those admissions into a closing deliverable, a price adjustment, or a specific indemnity.

Roughly AUD 4.1 million of known leakage or exposure (Riverlark ~3.2m, bonuses 0.42m + on-costs, Ironquay 0.18m, Sandbar 0.33m) sits in the Seller's draft without clear allocation to the Seller, against a headline price of 24m. That is before any valuation hit on Bluefen (30% of revenue) or DD-006.

---

## Part A — Liability architecture (clauses 8.3, 9.3, 12, 13, 20.5)

### A1. Fundamental and title warranties subjected to general caps and time limits — **reject outright**

The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties share the 20% cap and 18‑month period "for administrative simplicity". That is not a simplification; it is the single most buyer‑adverse term in the package.

- If title to the shares fails, we have paid AUD 24m for nothing. A recovery ceiling of AUD 4.8m is absurd for that risk.
- Market position (and what any Australian buyer would expect): title, capacity, authority and (usually) tax warranties capped at **100% of the purchase price** and surviving for the longer of the statutory limitation period or 6–7 years (tax: typically until expiry of the relevant assessment periods plus a margin).
- Note the disclosure letter paragraph 10: the Seller says title is "evidenced by the Company share register at DD‑012" and expressly notes that this "does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification." Read with clause 8.3, that is a set‑up: the Seller is laying the ground to argue that any title defect discoverable from the register or ASIC records was within our knowledge and is barred. Title must be an uncapped, un‑excludable warranty *and* backed by completion deliverables (executed transfers, register update, ASIC lodgement, share certificates or cancellation, no‑encumbrance confirmation).

**Ask:** Separate "Fundamental Warranties" (title, capacity, authority, no insolvency, solvency, share capital) — cap 100% of price, survive 7 years, excluded from basket/de minimis, excluded from knowledge qualifier and from disclosure. Tax warranties and tax indemnity — cap 100%, survive 7 years (or 4 years after end of the last relevant amendment period).

### A2. General cap at 20% (AUD 4.8m) — **negotiate up; acceptable only as part of a package**

20% is at the low end of the Australian mid‑market range (typically 20–50% for a company of this size with identified risk concentration). Given that 30% of revenue hinges on a single customer consent and there is an open privacy incident, we should open at 50% and expect to land at 30–35%, with specific indemnities sitting *outside* the cap (see Part B). If the Seller holds at 20%, the trade is W&I insurance with the Seller funding part of the premium, or a retention/escrow.

### A3. De minimis AUD 25,000 and basket AUD 250,000 (excess‑only) — **reduce and convert**

- De minimis of 25k on a 24m deal is roughly 0.1% — high but tolerable. Push to 10–15k and, critically, insist that **related claims aggregate** for de minimis purposes. Otherwise the three Sandbar renewals (3 × 110k) and a series of DD‑006 remediation costs can each be argued separately.
- Basket of 250k (~1.04%) is at the top of market. Push for 0.5–0.75%, and convert from "excess only" (deductible) to **"tipping"/first‑dollar** once exceeded.
- Confirm de minimis and basket **do not apply** to Fundamental, Tax, or specific indemnity claims, nor to the leakage/purchase‑price adjustment mechanics.

### A4. 18‑month claims period — **extend**

18 months is short for a software/analytics business where IP and data issues surface slowly. Ask for 24 months for general warranties (minimum: 18 months plus a window that captures at least one full audit cycle after Completion). Tax and Fundamental as per A1.

### A5. "Any limitation applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise" (cl 12.3/13) and "limitations, exclusive remedy and non‑reliance apply to all Claims of any nature" (cl 9.3/12.8/20.5) — **reject the drafting; carve out**

These are catch‑all provisions designed to sweep indemnities, covenants, leakage claims and even fraud into the capped regime. Required carve‑outs from *all* limitations:

1. Fraud, dishonesty, wilful concealment, wilful breach.
2. Fundamental and Tax Warranties / Tax Indemnity (own regime).
3. Specific indemnities (Part B) — subject only to their own caps, if any.
4. Leakage and purchase‑price adjustment claims (locked box or completion accounts mechanics must sit outside the cap and basket entirely).
5. Seller covenants (restraints, confidentiality, pre‑completion conduct, completion deliverables).
6. Liability that cannot be excluded at law — in particular, **statutory misleading or deceptive conduct claims** (Australian Consumer Law / ASIC Act). A clause purporting to exclude these is of doubtful enforceability but it will be run against us; make the carve‑out explicit.

Non‑reliance (20.5) must be mutual in effect — i.e., it should not operate to deny us reliance on the warranties, disclosure letter, or any management responses given in a formal Q&A process. Those should be expressly listed as reliance material.

Exclusive remedy (12.8) must not exclude injunctive relief, specific performance (critical for the completion deliverables in Part B), or rescission for fraud.

### A6. Buyer knowledge qualifier (cl 8.3) — **reject in the Seller's form**

As drafted, we lose any claim for any matter "discoverable from the data room or public records". That means:

- Every item the Seller has itself flagged in paragraphs 2–10 of the disclosure letter is, on the Seller's drafting, barred — including items the Seller admits are *unresolved* and unquantified (DD‑006, Ironquay, bonus on‑costs).
- "Discoverable" is a constructive‑knowledge standard; "advisers" extends it to things our lawyers *could* have found in ASIC searches. This is not market.
- It is an anti‑sandbagging clause at its most aggressive.

**Position:**

- Preferred: delete 8.3 entirely (pro‑sandbagging silence). Fall‑back: actual knowledge only, of a named deal team (3–4 individuals), of a matter *and* of the fact that it gives rise to a breach, and with no imputation from advisers.
- Whatever the knowledge standard, it must not apply to matters that are the subject of a specific indemnity — we know about those by definition; that is precisely why we are indemnifying them.

### A7. General disclosure of the data room and public registers (Schedule 7 / DL 1.1–1.2) — **reject; require fair disclosure standard**

Wholesale disclosure of an entire data room (DD‑002 to DD‑012) and of "publicly searchable corporate records" is not an acceptable disclosure standard. Require:

- Disclosure only of matters **fairly disclosed with sufficient detail to enable a reasonable buyer to identify the nature and scope of the matter**.
- Public registers: at most, ASIC company search and PPSR search against the Company as at a specified date, and only for the matters actually revealed on the face of those searches.
- Data room disclosed only against the warranties to which the document is relevant, by cross‑reference in the disclosure letter.
- Data room cut‑off at 22 September 2026 is fine, but documents loaded late, or buried in the wrong folder, must be flagged in a supplementary disclosure letter or not count.
- Paragraph 1.4 (no admission of breach, liability, materiality, or that anything is "legally required") is standard but must not be allowed to blunt the specific indemnities. We should respond in the SPA: "The Seller acknowledges that the matters in paragraphs 2–8 of the Disclosure Letter are the subject of the Specific Indemnities and that disclosure does not limit those indemnities."

Also note the Seller's reservation at paragraph 11: "The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement." Taken with 8.3 and 1.1, this is the Seller attempting to transfer the entire burden of diligence conclusions to us while retaining none of the risk. We should put on record (in correspondence, not just the SPA) that we are relying on the Seller's warranties and the specific indemnities, and that disclosure of a problem is not resolution of it.

---

## Part B — Identified exposures and how each should be allocated

### B1. Bluefen (DD‑002; ~AUD 3.6m, ~30% of FY26 revenue) — **make it a genuine condition precedent with teeth**

Seller position: "addressed"; reasonable endeavours; condition "satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent."

Problems:

- The disclosure letter admits no final written consent exists and no evidence that the clause 11.3 conditions have been satisfied. The Seller cannot describe the matter as "addressed".
- "Reasonable endeavours" is the weakest endeavours standard. For the customer that is 30% of revenue, we need "all reasonable endeavours" at minimum and ideally "best endeavours", with specific steps and reporting obligations.
- "Satisfied on delivery of written consent" is too loose: Bluefen could deliver a consent that is conditional, time‑limited, requires renegotiated pricing, or waives change‑control only in part.

**Ask:**

- CP (for the Buyer's sole benefit, waivable only by the Buyer): unconditional written consent from Bluefen under clause 11.2 in a form approved by the Buyer (acting reasonably), confirming the clause 11.3 conditions are satisfied or waived, with no amendment to commercial terms, and not withdrawn as at Completion.
- Buyer right to participate in communications with Bluefen; Seller not to make commitments on the Company's behalf without consent.
- If the consent is not obtained by the long‑stop date: Buyer may terminate, or elect to complete with a **price reduction** or **deferred/contingent consideration** tied to Bluefen revenue retention over 12–24 months (a 30% customer justifies this).
- Specific indemnity for loss if Bluefen terminates or materially reduces volumes within [12] months citing the change of control.
- Warranty: no notice (written or oral) from Bluefen of intention to terminate, reduce, re‑tender or renegotiate.

### B2. Riverlark Bank facility (DD‑003; ~AUD 3.2m) — **must be discharged at or before Completion; it is not a post‑Completion matter**

Seller position: release "to be provided following Completion."

This is inconsistent with the debt‑free/cash‑free basis. If the facility is still outstanding at Completion and the release arrives later, we have, in effect, paid AUD 24m *and* acquired AUD 3.2m of debt — a 13% price increase. Further, DD‑003 contains a change‑of‑control clause (8.1); completing without the bank's consent or repayment may trigger an event of default against the Company we now own.

**Ask:**

- Completion deliverable: executed deed of release and discharge of security from Riverlark, PPSR discharge (or undertaking to discharge within 2 business days with evidence), release of any guarantees given by the Company, and payout letter.
- Funds flow: repayment of the Riverlark payout figure **from the purchase price** at Completion, paid directly to Riverlark by the Buyer on the Seller's behalf. The Seller nets off; the Company closes debt‑free.
- If for any reason the facility is not repaid at Completion, a dollar‑for‑dollar price reduction and a Seller indemnity (uncapped) for all amounts owing, break costs and any default consequences.
- Confirm there are no other financial debts, hire purchase, guarantees or off‑balance‑sheet items under the "debt" definition — warranty plus completion certificate.

### B3. Closing bonuses (DD‑005; AUD 420,000 plus on‑costs) — **Seller cost, in the funds flow, grossed up**

Seller position: "a matter for the Seller and not separately itemised."

The bonuses are payable *by the Company* on Completion and continued employment. If they are not in the funds flow, the Company pays them post‑Completion from cash we have paid for — classic leakage. The disclosure letter openly admits they are not in the funds flow and that payroll tax, superannuation and on‑costs are unstated. Transaction bonuses typically attract superannuation guarantee (if OTE), payroll tax (NSW ~5.45%) and PAYG withholding; the all‑in cost is likely AUD 500–520k, not 420k.

**Ask:**

- Treat all Completion/transaction bonuses, plus employer superannuation, payroll tax and any other on‑costs, as **Transaction Costs / Debt‑like items** deducted from the price, or funded by the Seller into the Company at Completion with a specific line in the funds flow.
- Specific indemnity for any shortfall or any further transaction‑related payments to employees, advisers or management not reflected in the funds flow.
- Because the bonuses are conditioned on continued employment, clarify who bears the cost if the employee resigns before the pay date — it should not become a Buyer cost either way.
- Request the full list of recipients and terms; check for any change‑of‑control acceleration of options/ESOP or notice entitlements elsewhere.

### B4. Ironquay Development Studio (DD‑004 cl 7.3; DD‑010 shows AUD 180,000 open) — **title‑to‑IP issue, not a 180k issue**

Seller position: existing indemnity limited to the SOW3 payment and "considered adequate."

It is not adequate. Clause 7.3 conditions transfer of the SOW3 Project Materials on *cleared payment of every SOW3 fee*. If AUD 180,000 is unpaid, Paperbark does **not own** the SOW3 deliverables — Ironquay does. For an analytics business, that could be core product code. The exposure is not the 180k; it is (a) an IP title gap in the product, (b) Ironquay's leverage to demand more, (c) potential infringement claims for ongoing use, and (d) breach of the IP ownership warranties we would be giving to our own financiers or future buyers.

**Ask:**

- Completion deliverables: evidence of cleared payment of all SOW3 fees (bank confirmation, not just the ledger) **and** a confirmatory deed of assignment from Ironquay of all SOW3 Project Materials, including moral rights consents and source code delivery.
- If not available by Completion: price retention/escrow (say AUD 250–300k) released on delivery of the assignment, plus an uncapped specific indemnity for loss arising from any failure of title to or restriction on use of the SOW3 materials and any claim by Ironquay.
- Expand the indemnity beyond SOW3 — ask for IP‑ownership confirmation across all SOWs with Ironquay and any other contractor.
- IP warranties: Company owns or validly licenses all IP used in the business; all contractor‑developed IP has been assigned in writing; no open‑source copyleft contamination; source code escrow if relevant.

### B5. DD‑006 export / privacy incident — **not "preliminary and immaterial"; treat as live regulatory exposure**

Seller position: "preliminary operational matter… not expected to be material."

Facts the Seller itself discloses: a download link was sent to an unintended external email address; ~1,240 records of personal information (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps); unknown whether accessed; investigation incomplete; notification assessment not done.

Under the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) Notifiable Data Breaches scheme, an entity that suspects an eligible data breach must complete an assessment within 30 days and notify the OAIC and affected individuals if there is likely to be serious harm. The data (business contact details) is lower‑sensitivity, which helps, but the Seller has not done the assessment and the clock is running. The OAIC's enforcement posture and the penalty regime have hardened significantly since the 2022–2024 reforms. There may also be contractual notification obligations to the customer(s) whose users' data is involved — potentially Bluefen or Mossvale — which bears directly on B1.

**Ask:**

- Pre‑Completion covenant: Seller to procure that the Company completes the NDB assessment, documents it, obtains privacy counsel's opinion, and makes any required notifications before Completion; Buyer to receive copies and have approval rights over regulator and customer communications.
- Warranties: no other actual or suspected data breaches; compliance with APPs and contractual data obligations; no regulator correspondence.
- Specific indemnity (outside cap, basket and 8.3 knowledge qualifier) for all loss arising from the DD‑006 incident — regulator action, notification costs, customer claims or terminations, remediation, legal fees — surviving at least 6 years.
- Condition or termination right if the incident escalates to a confirmed breach involving a key customer before Completion.
- Check the Company's cyber insurance: notification given? Claim preserved? Policy survives change of control?

### B6. Sandbar supplier renewals (DD‑008, DD‑011; 3 × AUD 110,000) — **structure smell; investigate before conceding "ordinary course"**

Seller position: ordinary‑course operating costs.

The disclosure letter undercuts the Seller's own position: it says the three renewals must be "read together for timing/scope" and expressly declines to say whether they are "unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course." Three identical AUD 110k commitments, split across two data‑room documents, each just over 4× the de minimis — this looks like a single AUD 330k commitment fragmented, either to stay beneath approval thresholds or to defeat the de minimis if claimed individually.

**Ask:**

- Full copies of all three renewals, signing dates, approval records, and board/management authority. Were they entered after the locked‑box date or during the exclusivity period? If so, they are potentially leakage or breach of pre‑Completion conduct covenants.
- Confirm whether the services are needed; whether they are terminable; whether the counterparties are related to the Seller or management (related‑party warranty).
- If not demonstrably ordinary course and necessary, treat as leakage / price reduction, or require the Seller to procure termination without cost.
- Ensure de minimis aggregation language (A3) captures related claims.

### B7. Office lease (DD‑007) and Mossvale (DD‑009) — **lower priority but close out**

- Lease: a notification obligation on change of control is usually straightforward, but a missed notification can be a default. Make it a pre‑Completion covenant with evidence of delivery as a Completion deliverable; warranty of no landlord default or dispute.
- Mossvale: the Seller is correct that a restriction on *assignment* is not usually triggered by a share sale. But check for any "change of control" definition elsewhere in the contract, any key‑person or ownership representations, and any most‑favoured‑customer or exclusivity terms. Confirm Mossvale's revenue contribution; if it is a top‑5 customer, add it to the Bluefen‑style no‑notice warranty.

### B8. Tax and IP "settled under the general regime" — **not accepted**

The Seller's one‑liner is a placeholder for "no tax indemnity, no separate IP regime." For a software company with contractor‑developed IP (Ironquay) and a debt facility, we need:

- Full tax indemnity (pre‑Completion tax, uncapped or 100% of price, 7‑year survival), including GST, payroll tax (relevant to B3), R&D tax incentive clawback risk, and Division 7A/related‑party items.
- Tax warranties outside the general cap and knowledge qualifier.
- IP as above (B4): ownership, assignment chain, no infringement, open‑source compliance, data rights in the analytics datasets.

### B9. Title (DD‑012) — see A1. Add: ASIC and PPSR searches as at Completion; Seller to deliver signed transfers, register updates, resignation/appointments, and a solvency/no‑encumbrance warranty. The disclaimer that we have not verified title is the Seller's problem to cure with warranties, not ours to absorb.

---

## Part C — Structural protections to put on the table

Given the number of unresolved items the Seller has itself identified, we should not rely on warranty claims alone:

1. **Retention / escrow**: 10–15% of price (AUD 2.4–3.6m) held for 18–24 months to secure warranty and indemnity claims. Alternatively, W&I insurance with Seller‑funded premium (noting known issues — Bluefen, DD‑006, Ironquay — will be excluded from cover, which is exactly why they need standalone indemnities and escrow).
2. **Price mechanics**: if locked box, lock the box date, define leakage to include the bonuses, Sandbar renewals (if post‑date) and any Riverlark non‑repayment; if completion accounts, ensure debt definition captures Riverlark, accrued bonuses and on‑costs. Debt‑free/cash‑free must be given mechanical effect, not just recited.
3. **Specific indemnities register** — outside cap, basket, time limits and knowledge qualifier:
   - Riverlark non‑discharge / default
   - Transaction bonuses and on‑costs
   - Ironquay IP title and claims
   - DD‑006 incident
   - Bluefen change‑of‑control loss (or contingent consideration)
   - Pre‑Completion tax
4. **Completion deliverables checklist** — Bluefen consent, Riverlark release/PPSR discharge, Ironquay payment evidence + assignment, lease notification, DD‑006 assessment report, share transfer documents.
5. **Long‑stop date and termination rights** for failure of CPs, MAC (including loss or notice from Bluefen, or regulatory action on DD‑006).
6. **Information covenant** between signing and Completion: weekly updates on Bluefen, Riverlark, DD‑006; no new supplier commitments over AUD 25k without consent.

---

## Summary of recommendations

| # | Issue | Seller position | Our position | Priority |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Fundamental/title warranties | Same cap & period as general | 100% of price; 7 years; outside basket, disclosure and knowledge qualifier | Critical |
| 2 | Buyer knowledge (8.3) | Constructive knowledge incl. advisers, data room, public records | Delete; fallback actual knowledge of named individuals, not applicable to indemnified matters | Critical |
| 3 | Riverlark AUD 3.2m | Release after Completion | Repaid from price at Completion; release & PPSR discharge as deliverables; uncapped indemnity | Critical |
| 4 | Bluefen consent (30% revenue) | "Addressed"; reasonable endeavours | Buyer‑only CP, unconditional consent in approved form; all reasonable/best endeavours; price adjustment or deferred consideration if not obtained; indemnity | Critical |
| 5 | Limitations apply to all Claims | Catch‑all | Carve out fraud, Fundamental, Tax, specific indemnities, leakage, covenants, non‑excludable statutory claims; equitable remedies preserved | Critical |
| 6 | Closing bonuses AUD 420k | Not in funds flow | Seller cost incl. super/payroll tax; in funds flow as price deduction; indemnity | High |
| 7 | Ironquay IP | SOW3 payment indemnity "adequate" | Payment evidence + confirmatory assignment as deliverables; escrow; uncapped IP title indemnity; broader IP warranties | High |
| 8 | DD‑006 incident | Preliminary, immaterial | Pre‑Completion NDB assessment and notifications; specific indemnity outside cap/knowledge; MAC trigger | High |
| 9 | General disclosure | Whole data room + public registers | Fair‑disclosure standard; specific cross‑referenced disclosure; limited searches only | High |
| 10 | General cap 20% | AUD 4.8m | Open 50%, land 30–35%; or W&I + escrow | High |
| 11 | De minimis/basket | 25k / 250k deductible | 10–15k with aggregation / 0.5–0.75% tipping | Medium |
| 12 | Claims period | 18 months | 24 months general; 7 years Fundamental & Tax | Medium |
| 13 | Sandbar renewals | Ordinary course | Full diligence; leakage/price reduction unless demonstrably necessary and pre‑existing | Medium |
| 14 | Tax/IP regimes | "Settled" under general regime | Standalone tax indemnity and tax/IP warranties outside general cap | Medium |
| 15 | Lease / Mossvale | Notification only / no consent | Covenants and deliverables; confirm no CoC triggers | Low |
| 16 | Escrow/security | None offered | 10–15% retention 18–24 months or W&I with Seller‑funded premium | High |

**Recommended next steps:** (1) Issue a mark‑up that re‑cuts the liability regime per Part A before engaging on individual items — the Seller's package only works for them if 8.3 and the "all Claims" sweep survive. (2) Send a focused information request: Bluefen correspondence, Riverlark payout letter, Ironquay payment evidence, bonus schedule with on‑costs, DD‑006 investigation file and insurer notification, the three Sandbar agreements with signing dates. (3) Have the valuation team model a Bluefen‑loss scenario and a Riverlark‑not‑repaid scenario so we go into the call with the price impact in hand. (4) Put on record, in correspondence, that we are relying on the warranties and specific indemnities notwithstanding the Seller's reservation at paragraph 11.

I'm happy to turn any of the above into SPA drafting or a rider to the disclosure letter response.
